say: This is Interlock. It coordinates AI agents that change production systems, and it runs on a FalkorDB graph.

Companies now run many agents at the same time. Agent A migrates the orders database. Agent B deploys the payments service. The two tasks look unrelated. But the dependency graph shows a link: both changes reach checkout, and customers use checkout. If both changes run together, checkout fails. The logs show two changes, and nobody can say which one caused the failure.

Engineers report this on Reddit. An agent deleted a production database. Security teams ask who approved a command, and how to prove what it did. A prompt cannot fix this, because one agent cannot see the others.

Interlock sits outside the agents. Each agent asks Interlock before it acts. Interlock walks the graph and finds the overlap at checkout, so agent B waits. When agent A finishes, Interlock wakes agent B, and B deploys. Both decisions are stored in the graph.

This is the live console. Twenty-four agents change a simulated online store. Each card is a service, a database, a topic or a flag. Green cards are changes in progress. Amber cards are inside a change's impact zone. Dashed cards wait for another change. The dark tags show which agent holds each lock.
Every answer says why. This change waits for another agent. The panel shows its impact zone, the human who authorised the agent, each decision, and the Cypher query behind it.
Now turn enforcement off. The agents act without asking, and red collisions start within seconds.
In our benchmark, one hundred and ninety-seven of two hundred and fifty-five changes collided without Interlock. With Interlock, none did. The cost is an average wait of thirty seconds.

Policies live in the graph too. A staging bot tries to delete a production database, and Interlock blocks it. A sub-agent with no human behind it tries to deploy payments, and Interlock blocks that too. A migration of the payments database waits for a human, and Arjun approves it here.
Here, two agents each hold one resource and wait for the other's. Interlock finds the cycle in the waits-on graph and rolls back the less urgent agent.

Everything is one FalkorDB graph: resources and their dependencies, teams, people, agents, intents and decisions. The impact zone is a reverse walk over depends-on edges. One Cypher write checks for conflicts and takes the lock atomically, so two agents can never both win. The audit trail is the same graph.
Any agent can use Interlock over MCP or plain HTTP. Claude Code asks before it deploys, waits when it must, and releases the lock when it is done.
That is Interlock, built on FalkorDB for Graph Hacks. Thank you for watching.
